title: The Life of Albert Einstein
passages: ALBERT EINSTEIN was born on March 14, 1879, in the German city of ULM. A year later his family moved to MUNICH, where his father and uncle started a company making electrical equipment. As a small boy Albert was slow to start talking, and his parents worried about him. He liked quiet, patient games such as PUZZLES, BLOCKS, and CARDS, which he stacked into tall towers.

When he was about 5 years old, Albert was ill in bed and his father showed him a COMPASS. However the case was turned, the needle swung back to point north. Albert was amazed that an invisible force could move it, and he remembered the moment all his life. Music mattered too. His mother had him learn the VIOLIN, which he played for the rest of his life, and he loved the music of MOZART, BACH, and SCHUBERT.

Albert found his school in Munich, the LUITPOLD GYMNASIUM, strict and dull. Lessons depended on memorising facts and obeying teachers. He did far better when he studied alone, and by his teens he had taught himself GEOMETRY, ALGEBRA, and CALCULUS from books. In 1894 his family moved to ITALY for business, and soon Albert left the school as well.

Albert set his heart on the SWISS FEDERAL POLYTECHNIC in ZURICH. He failed its entrance exam in 1895, yet he scored highly in mathematics and physics, so he spent a year at a school in AARAU and was admitted in 1896. That same year he gave up his German citizenship. He graduated in 1900 and later became a citizen of SWITZERLAND.

After graduating, Albert could not find a university job. In 1902 he began work at the PATENT OFFICE in BERN, checking new inventions to see whether they would really work. The job was STEADY, QUIET, and SAFE, and it left his mind free to wander. He said later that some of his finest ideas came to him at his desk there.

In 1905, at just 26, he published four papers that changed physics. Between them they dealt with LIGHT, ATOMS, MOTION, and ENERGY, and they included SPECIAL RELATIVITY and the famous equation E = mc². In it, c stands for the speed of light, about 300,000,000 metres per second. Scientists call 1905 his ANNUS MIRABILIS, which is Latin for miracle year.

Special relativity dealt only with steady motion. For ten more years Einstein wrestled with a harder problem: GRAVITY. In 1915 he completed his theory of GENERAL RELATIVITY. It said that heavy objects bend SPACE and TIME around them, and that this bending is what we feel as the pull of gravity.

The theory made a bold prediction: starlight passing close to the SUN should be bent. In 1919 British astronomers photographed stars during a total ECLIPSE and found the light had bent by the amount Einstein predicted. Almost overnight he became FAMOUS, ADMIRED, and CELEBRATED around the world. Light itself is fast but not instant: sunlight takes about 500 seconds to reach Earth, travelling at about 300,000 kilometres per second.

By 1914 Einstein had taught at universities in BERN, ZURICH, and PRAGUE, and he then moved to BERLIN. In 1922 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1921. Surprisingly, it was not awarded for relativity. It honoured his services to theoretical physics and especially his explanation of the photoelectric effect, from one of his 1905 papers.

In 1933 the NAZIS came to power in Germany. Einstein, who was Jewish, was abroad at the time and never went back. The new government seized his HOUSE, his BOAT, and his SAVINGS. He settled at the INSTITUTE FOR ADVANCED STUDY in Princeton, New Jersey, became an American citizen in 1940, and worked there until his death in 1955.

In 1939 scientists learned that splitting URANIUM atoms could release enormous energy. Fearing that Nazi Germany might build a bomb, Einstein signed a letter to President Franklin ROOSEVELT warning him of the danger. The letter helped start the American effort that built the first ATOMIC bomb, though Einstein himself did not work on it. He later called signing it a great mistake, and for the rest of his life he spoke out for PEACE, FREEDOM, and EQUALITY.

In 1952 Israel offered him the post of president. He was deeply moved but declined, saying he lacked the experience to deal with people and official duties. Days before his death he signed the RUSSELL-EINSTEIN MANIFESTO, which called on LEADERS, SCIENTISTS, and CITIZENS to settle disputes without war. He died in Princeton on April 18, 1955, aged 76.
